286
00:15:27.870 --> 00:15:30.990
so where it gets points, how to avoid bumping into walls,

287
00:15:30.990 --> 00:15:33.210
where it loses points, and furniture,

288
00:15:33.210 --> 00:15:34.800
and which parts are more efficient.

289
00:15:34.800 --> 00:15:37.320
So over time, the robot vacuum cleaner

290
00:15:37.320 --> 00:15:38.820
will become more efficient

291
00:15:38.820 --> 00:15:40.930
by working out where it gets rewards

292
00:15:41.820 --> 00:15:43.220
and where it gets penalties.

293
00:15:46.410 --> 00:15:49.170
In machine learning, some data is used to train the model

294
00:15:49.170 --> 00:15:51.303
and some is set aside to test the model.

295
00:15:53.910 --> 00:15:56.010
So we've got two types of data,

296
00:15:56.010 --> 00:15:58.833
we've got training data and testing data.

297
00:16:01.080 --> 00:16:03.030
Note that testing data is used by developers

298
00:16:03.030 --> 00:16:05.913
to check the model works as intended after training.

299
00:16:10.380 --> 00:16:11.610
Time for a question.

300
00:16:11.610 --> 00:16:14.640
Machine learning is A, a way for computers

301
00:16:14.640 --> 00:16:17.250
to follow step-by-step instructions,

302
00:16:17.250 --> 00:16:20.550
B, a method in which computers identify patterns in data

303
00:16:20.550 --> 00:16:22.320
and adjust their outputs,

304
00:16:22.320 --> 00:16:24.723
or C, a machine that copies human thoughts?

305
00:16:29.490 --> 00:16:31.200
Well done, machine learning is B,

306
00:16:31.200 --> 00:16:34.050
a method in which computers identify patterns in data

307
00:16:34.050 --> 00:16:35.703
and adjust their outputs.

308
00:16:38.370 --> 00:16:40.710
Another question, what does machine learning need

309
00:16:40.710 --> 00:16:42.180
to work well?

310
00:16:42.180 --> 00:16:44.700
Is it A, lots of data and examples,

311
00:16:44.700 --> 00:16:48.813
B, a strong internet connection, or C, batteries and wires?

312
00:16:54.240 --> 00:16:56.490
Well done, the correct answer is A,

313
00:16:56.490 --> 00:16:59.460
machine learning needs lots of data and examples

314
00:16:59.460 --> 00:17:00.753
in order to work well.

315
00:17:03.420 --> 00:17:05.940
Another question, supervised learning is learning,

316
00:17:05.940 --> 00:17:10.830
A, by copying other machines, B, by trial and error only,

317
00:17:10.830 --> 00:17:13.983
or C, with examples and correct answers?

318
00:17:19.740 --> 00:17:21.360
Well done, the answer is C,

319
00:17:21.360 --> 00:17:23.760
supervised learning is learning with examples

320
00:17:23.760 --> 00:17:25.173
and correct answers.

321
00:17:29.160 --> 00:17:31.770
Unsupervised learning is when the machine is,

322
00:17:31.770 --> 00:17:34.080
A, given no data,

323
00:17:34.080 --> 00:17:36.830
B, finds pattern in data without answers,

324
00:17:36.830 --> 00:17:39.063
or C, memorises all data?

325
00:17:45.270 --> 00:17:46.680
Well done, the answer is B,

326
00:17:46.680 --> 00:17:48.390
unsupervised learning is when the machine

327
00:17:48.390 --> 00:17:50.853
finds patterns in data without answers.

328
00:17:54.030 --> 00:17:55.950
Reinforcement learning is when the machine,

329
00:17:55.950 --> 00:17:58.350
A, adjust its behaviour through trial and error

330
00:17:58.350 --> 00:17:59.910
and receives feedback,

331
00:17:59.910 --> 00:18:03.090
B, identifies patterns in data without answers,

332
00:18:03.090 --> 00:18:06.573
or C, is directly programmed by humans to complete a task?

333
00:18:12.076 --> 00:18:13.920
And Well done, the answer is A,

334
00:18:13.920 --> 00:18:16.170
reinforcement learning is when the machine adjusts

335
00:18:16.170 --> 00:18:19.473
its behaviour through trial and error and receives feedback.

336
00:18:22.800 --> 00:18:25.350
Now, time for your task B.

337
00:18:25.350 --> 00:18:26.880
Match the type of machine learning

338
00:18:26.880 --> 00:18:28.350
to the correct description.

339
00:18:28.350 --> 00:18:30.540
So we've got three types of machine learning,

340
00:18:30.540 --> 00:18:32.910
supervised learning, unsupervised learning,

341
00:18:32.910 --> 00:18:34.680
and reinforcement learning,

342
00:18:34.680 --> 00:18:35.760
and three descriptions,

343
00:18:35.760 --> 00:18:38.100
so the first description, the machine groups

344
00:18:38.100 --> 00:18:41.310
and organises the data without humans directly programming

345
00:18:41.310 --> 00:18:43.920
to find useful hidden patterns.

346
00:18:43.920 --> 00:18:46.440
The second description, the machine adjusts its behaviour

347
00:18:46.440 --> 00:18:49.230
by trying to do a task and getting feedback.

348
00:18:49.230 --> 00:18:51.810
And the final description, uses known answers

349
00:18:51.810 --> 00:18:53.610
to train the machine learning model.

350
00:18:58.440 --> 00:19:00.540
So let's have a look at how those link up.

351
00:19:01.410 --> 00:19:03.720
So supervised learning uses known answers

352
00:19:03.720 --> 00:19:05.520
to train the machine learning model,

353
00:19:06.390 --> 00:19:08.490
unsupervised learning, the machine groups

354
00:19:08.490 --> 00:19:11.250
and organises the data without humans directly programming

355
00:19:11.250 --> 00:19:13.140
to find useful hidden patterns,

356
00:19:13.140 --> 00:19:15.293
and finally, reinforcement learning is when the machine

357
00:19:15.293 --> 00:19:17.927
adjusts its behaviour by trying to do a task

358
00:19:17.927 --> 00:19:19.473
and getting feedback.

359
00:19:22.800 --> 00:19:25.170
Second part of your task, in your own words,

360
00:19:25.170 --> 00:19:28.143
write two or three sentences to describe machine learning.

361
00:19:34.410 --> 00:19:36.480
And you could have written something like this.

362
00:19:36.480 --> 00:19:39.270
So machine learning, or ML, is part of AI

363
00:19:39.270 --> 00:19:41.940
that helps computers get better at completing a task

364
00:19:41.940 --> 00:19:44.220
over time by using data.

365
00:19:44.220 --> 00:19:46.020
With ML, the computer uses data

366
00:19:46.020 --> 00:19:48.000
to adjust how it performs tasks

367
00:19:48.000 --> 00:19:49.110
rather than being programmed

368
00:19:49.110 --> 00:19:51.330
with fixed rules for each task.

369
00:19:51.330 --> 00:19:53.280
There are different types of ML models,

370
00:19:53.280 --> 00:19:55.315
but they all share some common features,

371
00:19:55.315 --> 00:19:57.240
such as working with training data,

372
00:19:57.240 --> 00:19:59.400
identifying patterns or relationships,

373
00:19:59.400 --> 00:20:01.623
and making predictions on new data.

374
00:20:05.580 --> 00:20:08.070
We can now move on to the third learning cycle

375
00:20:08.070 --> 00:20:08.903
in this lesson,

376
00:20:08.903 --> 00:20:11.463
which is to compare machine learning and programming.

377
00:20:15.390 --> 00:20:17.047
So Sam's observed through this lesson that,

378
00:20:17.047 --> 00:20:19.080
"Machine learning sounds useful,

379
00:20:19.080 --> 00:20:21.270
but how is it different to traditional programming,"

380
00:20:21.270 --> 00:20:22.570
which is a great question.

381
00:20:23.910 --> 00:20:25.680
And Andeep says, "In traditional programming,

382
00:20:25.680 --> 00:20:30.110
every rule is written by a human for a computer to follow."

383
00:20:30.110 --> 00:20:31.230
In machine learning,

384
00:20:31.230 --> 00:20:33.900
the machine form its own rules from data.

385
00:20:33.900 --> 00:20:35.463
So that's the key difference.

386
00:20:38.430 --> 00:20:41.340
Although machine learning models figure out rules from data,

387
00:20:41.340 --> 00:20:43.803
human programmers still write the initial code,

388
00:20:46.410 --> 00:20:49.680
and Andeep says, "Humans also decide what ML model to use,

389
00:20:49.680 --> 00:20:52.107
how to train it, and which settings to use."

390
00:20:54.720 --> 00:20:57.090
Humans select and clean the data, check results,

391
00:20:57.090 --> 00:20:59.583
and make sure the model is working as intended.

392
00:21:00.450 --> 00:21:03.513
So in machine learning, there are key roles for humans.

393
00:21:05.130 --> 00:21:06.120
To work effectively,

394
00:21:06.120 --> 00:21:08.730
machine learning models need large amounts of data

395
00:21:08.730 --> 00:21:10.233
to develop their own rules.

396
00:21:13.500 --> 00:21:15.210
The more examples of model sees,

397
00:21:15.210 --> 00:21:18.573
the better it can spot patterns and make actual predictions.

398
00:21:22.080 --> 00:21:24.600
In traditional programming, the rules are written by humans,

399
00:21:24.600 --> 00:21:27.060
so very little data is needed.

400
00:21:27.060 --> 00:21:28.350
That's highlighted by the fact

401
00:21:28.350 --> 00:21:30.150
in machine learning, you have lots of data,

402
00:21:30.150 --> 00:21:32.640
so a big representation of the word data,

403
00:21:32.640 --> 00:21:34.470
and in traditional programming, it's more about rules,

404
00:21:34.470 --> 00:21:37.323
so a much smaller representation of the word data.

405
00:21:40.770 --> 00:21:41.850
In machine learning,

406
00:21:41.850 --> 00:21:44.100
the machine can improve its own performance

407
00:21:44.100 --> 00:21:46.113
as it uses more or better data.

408
00:21:47.700 --> 00:21:48.810
In traditional programming,

409
00:21:48.810 --> 00:21:52.173
improvements are only made if a human updates the code.

410
00:21:57.000 --> 00:21:58.170
With traditional programming,

411
00:21:58.170 --> 00:22:01.803
it can be hard to solve complex or unclear problems.

412
00:22:05.910 --> 00:22:07.320
However, in contrast,

413
00:22:07.320 --> 00:22:09.660
machine learning can help solve complex problems

414
00:22:09.660 --> 00:22:11.700
by learning patterns in huge amounts of data

415
00:22:11.700 --> 00:22:14.013
that will be hard for humans to understand.

416
00:22:19.110 --> 00:22:21.843
Traditional code follows clear steps to do its job,

417
00:22:25.170 --> 00:22:27.030
and Sam says, "In a calculator,

418
00:22:27.030 --> 00:22:30.027
code directly tells it how to add or subtract."

419
00:22:31.530 --> 00:22:33.960
Traditional code is great for tasks with known rules,

420
00:22:33.960 --> 00:22:36.903
like converting units or working out calculations.

421
00:22:38.490 --> 00:22:41.433
It's transparent, predictable, and easy to debug.

422
00:22:45.360 --> 00:22:47.730
With machine learning, it can be hard to understand

423
00:22:47.730 --> 00:22:49.833
why the machine makes certain decisions,

424
00:22:52.470 --> 00:22:55.140
and Sam says, "It's not possible to go into the ML model

425
00:22:55.140 --> 00:22:57.687
and clearly see how it learned from the data."

426
00:23:00.540 --> 00:23:02.400
So this means you can't really debug

427
00:23:02.400 --> 00:23:03.420
a machine learning model

428
00:23:03.420 --> 00:23:06.000
in the same way you debug normal code.

429
00:23:06.000 --> 00:23:08.277
So that's a key difference between programming

430
00:23:08.277 --> 00:23:09.513
and machine learning.

431
00:23:13.050 --> 00:23:15.900
The table below shows some key features that can be used

432
00:23:15.900 --> 00:23:18.700
to compare traditional programming and machine learning.

433
00:23:21.870 --> 00:23:24.390
So let's look across the table, so how it works.

434
00:23:24.390 --> 00:23:25.770
Traditional programming works

435
00:23:25.770 --> 00:23:28.410
by a programmer writing the rules manually.

436
00:23:28.410 --> 00:23:30.060
In machine learning, a model learns

437
00:23:30.060 --> 00:23:32.823
or adjust its output based on the rules from the data.

438
00:23:33.870 --> 00:23:36.480
So what's the role of data in those two different things?

439
00:23:36.480 --> 00:23:39.540
So in traditional programming, data is used as an input.

440
00:23:39.540 --> 00:23:41.823
Small amounts are often enough.

441
00:23:42.960 --> 00:23:45.090
In machine learning, the role of data is needed

442
00:23:45.090 --> 00:23:47.283
in large amounts to train and improve.

443
00:23:48.930 --> 00:23:50.643
So how do they improve over time?

444
00:23:51.480 --> 00:23:54.360
Traditional programming only changes if a human updates

445
00:23:54.360 --> 00:23:57.060
the code, whereas machine learning can improve

446
00:23:57.060 --> 00:23:59.160
with more or better data.

447
00:23:59.160 --> 00:24:02.730
And finally, how does it handle complex tasks?

448
00:24:02.730 --> 00:24:04.680
Well, in traditional programming, it can be difficult

449
00:24:04.680 --> 00:24:07.680
to code for complex or unclear problems,

450
00:24:07.680 --> 00:24:09.900
whereas machine learning is good at learning patterns

451
00:24:09.900 --> 00:24:13.563
in hard tasks like images, speech, or data.

452
00:24:17.250 --> 00:24:18.750
Time for some questions.

453
00:24:18.750 --> 00:24:22.245
Traditional programing works by A, learning from examples,

454
00:24:22.245 --> 00:24:24.333
B, guessing what the user wants,

455
00:24:25.380 --> 00:24:28.173
or C, using fixed rules written by a programmer?

456
00:24:32.730 --> 00:24:34.830
Well done, the answer is C,

457
00:24:34.830 --> 00:24:37.953
it works by using fixed rules written by a programmer.

458
00:24:41.490 --> 00:24:43.980
Machine learning is different from traditional programming

459
00:24:43.980 --> 00:24:46.560
because it A, improves by adjusting its output

460
00:24:46.560 --> 00:24:48.030
based on data,

461
00:24:48.030 --> 00:24:50.190
B, works without a computer,

462
00:24:50.190 --> 00:24:52.533
or C only works for math problems?

463
00:24:57.390 --> 00:24:58.460
And the answer is, A,

464
00:24:58.460 --> 00:25:02.073
it improves by adjusting its output based on data.

465
00:25:05.580 --> 00:25:06.780
True or false?

466
00:25:06.780 --> 00:25:08.610
Is it easy to understand the decisions

467
00:25:08.610 --> 00:25:12.450
made by machine learning models and they are easy to debug?

468
00:25:12.450 --> 00:25:14.013
Is that true or false?

469
00:25:19.230 --> 00:25:20.880
Well done. The answer is false.

470
00:25:20.880 --> 00:25:22.233
Can you explain why?

471
00:25:28.530 --> 00:25:30.480
And it's because it can be hard to understand

472
00:25:30.480 --> 00:25:32.940
why machine learning models make certain decisions,

473
00:25:32.940 --> 00:25:34.830
and you can't debug a machine learning model

474
00:25:34.830 --> 00:25:37.413
in the same way you debug normal code.

475
00:25:42.540 --> 00:25:45.427
So for task C, Jun has a question.

476
00:25:45.427 --> 00:25:48.720
"How are machine learning and programming different?"

477
00:25:48.720 --> 00:25:50.940
And this prompt to help you, in your own words,

478
00:25:50.940 --> 00:25:53.520
compare some of the differences between machine learning

479
00:25:53.520 --> 00:25:54.873
and programming to Jun.

480
00:26:02.160 --> 00:26:04.560
So you could have written something like this.

481
00:26:04.560 --> 00:26:06.480
Machine learning and traditional programming

482
00:26:06.480 --> 00:26:09.690
are different ways of getting computers to solve problems.

483
00:26:09.690 --> 00:26:12.330
In traditional programming, a human writes the rules

484
00:26:12.330 --> 00:26:15.030
and the computer follows them exactly.

485
00:26:15.030 --> 00:26:16.710
It works well when the rules are clear

486
00:26:16.710 --> 00:26:18.033
and don't change much.

487
00:26:18.900 --> 00:26:20.340
Machine learning is different

488
00:26:20.340 --> 00:26:21.810
because instead of writing the rules,

489
00:26:21.810 --> 00:26:23.850
we give the computer lots of data

490
00:26:23.850 --> 00:26:27.300
and let it identify the patterns without human help.

491
00:26:27.300 --> 00:26:29.610
This makes ML better for complex tasks,

492
00:26:29.610 --> 00:26:31.710
where writing rules will be too difficult.

493
00:26:33.000 --> 00:26:34.860
Another difference is that traditional programming

494
00:26:34.860 --> 00:26:38.640
is transparent, predictable, and easy to debug.

495
00:26:38.640 --> 00:26:40.620
However, you can't debug a machine learning model

496
00:26:40.620 --> 00:26:42.753
in the same way you debug normal code.

497
00:26:46.475 --> 00:26:48.330
Here's a summary of this lesson,

498
00:26:48.330 --> 00:26:50.913
Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence.

499
00:26:52.260 --> 00:26:54.540
Artificial intelligence is about computer systems

500
00:26:54.540 --> 00:26:56.670
that adjust their behaviour based on data

501
00:26:56.670 --> 00:26:59.580
or follow rules to perform complex tasks.

502
00:26:59.580 --> 00:27:02.040
Machine learning is a type of artificial intelligence

503
00:27:02.040 --> 00:27:05.040
where computers adjust their behaviour based on data

504
00:27:05.040 --> 00:27:07.040
and improve their performance over time.

505
00:27:07.980 --> 00:27:10.260
Machine learning is different from traditional programming

506
00:27:10.260 --> 00:27:12.540
because it identifies rules from data

507
00:27:12.540 --> 00:27:15.393
instead of being programmed what to do by a human.

508
00:27:19.320 --> 00:27:21.330
Thank you for joining me for this lesson,

509
00:27:21.330 --> 00:27:23.880
and well done for all the hard work you've put in.

510
00:27:23.880 --> 00:27:25.920
I do hope to see you again in the near future

511
00:27:25.920 --> 00:27:27.963
in another Oak National Academy lesson.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Data science is used to make smarter decisions.
Data scientists analyse data to find patterns and discover useful information.
Data can be cleaned and organised to make it more useful.
Data can be biased if it doesn’t represent everyone fairly.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Data science isn’t just about gathering data, it’s about understanding data and using it to make decisions or discoveries.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Data science is just about collecting loads of data.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe data science and explain how data is used to make decisions.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Use real-world relatable examples with learners. Ask them to consider how managers decide on which players to choose for their favourite sports team or how a streaming service knows what shows to recommend.

lessons.transcript_sentences:
Welcome to this Oak National Academy lesson, which is called Data science, and it's taken from the unit Computer systems and data science.
Thank you for joining me for this lesson today, and I look forward to learning along with you.
The outcome of today's lesson is, I can describe data science and explain how data is used to make decisions.
We have four keywords or phrases in this lesson.
So, the first one is analyze, and analyze means to look at something carefully to understand it better.
Then we have data pattern.
A data pattern is a recurring trend, relationship, or structure found within a set of data.
Next, we have data cleaning.
And data cleaning means fixing or removing mistakes in data to make it correct and ready to use.
And finally, we have data bias, so data bias is when data is unfair or unbalanced, which can lead to wrong or unfair results.
So, there's our four key words or phrases, analyze, data pattern, data cleaning, and data bias.
There's two learning cycles in this lesson, so the first learning cycle is to describe data science, and we'll start that in a minute.
And the second learning cycle is explain how data is used to make decisions.
So, let's begin that first learning cycle, describe data science.
Sam has a question for Jun, "Have you ever wondered how video streaming services seem to know what you like to watch?" And Jun says, "I think that's data science in action, Sam." So let's see what he means.
Data science is all about using data like numbers and facts to solve problems and make smart decisions.
And it's a bit like being a detective.
So, just like a detective will use data like numbers and facts to solve a case, data scientists collect, prepare, and analyze data to discover data patterns and answers.
Data science is used in the real world every day in lots of different ways.
Let's have a look at some examples.
So, Sam has an example.
"Companies use data science to understand their customers, make smart business choices, and save time and money." So, there's lots of uses of data science in that statement there, and we'll look at some examples of those as we go through this lesson.
So, here's the first example.
Professional sports teams use data science a lot.
So, "Coaches and managers," as Sam points out, "can track player statistics to improve player performance and choose the best team." And they can do that across a whole multitude of sports.
So, here we have basketball, football, and tennis.
So, in team sports, they can monitor players to make sure they're contributing to the team and performing their role correctly.
In individual sports, they can look at technique, fitness, and all sorts of things.
There's so many different ways sports teams can use data science to improve performance.
Doctors and healthcare workers also use data science.
"Doctors can diagnose and treat patients more accurately.
They can also track, predict, and prevent health problems." So, this is a real way in which data science is making it a proper impact on people's lives and wellbeing.
There are many other examples of how data science is used in modern life, and these include weather forecasting to predict storms, rain, sunshine, using data from satellites.
Traffic apps use data to show the fastest route.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Every computer has the same basic parts such as a processor, memory, and storage.
The central processing unit (CPU) executes instructions and controls other parts of a computer system.
All computers use the fetch, decode, execute cycle as the basic way they execute programs.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The CPU is an important part of a computer system but a computer also needs memory, input, output, and storage to work properly. All parts must work together as a system.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The CPU is the only important part of a computer.

lessons.transcript_sentences:
Hi, my name is Mr. Hall, and welcome to this Oak National Academy lesson, which is called Computer Architecture, and it's taken from the unit Computer Systems and Data Science.
I'm delighted you've joined me for this lesson today, so let's get started.
Today's learning outcome is, "I can describe the parts of a computer system and explain how they work together to execute programs." We've got four keywords in this lesson.
First keyword is processor, and processor is the part of the computer that carries out instructions and makes decisions.
So that's the processor.
Secondly, we've got Random Access Memory or RAM.
So Random Access Memory is where the computer temporarily stores data and instructions it's using.
Next, we've got storage.
So storage is where the computer keeps data and files permanently even when it's turned off.
And finally, we have execute.
So execute is to carry out a program or a set of instructions on a computer.
So there's our four keywords or phrases: processor, Random Access Memory or RAM, storage, and execute.
We've got two learning cycles in this lesson.
So the first learning cycle, which we'll start in a minute, is to describe parts of a computer.

Describe parts of a computer.
So Laura's got a question for Jun and she's asking, "Do you know what parts all computers have in common?" And Jun says, "Well, there are so many different types of computer, but I think they all must have processor, memory, and storage." So let's see if they're right.
Jun is correct.
All computing systems need a processor, memory, and storage.
So the processor is sometimes called the CPU and the memory is where things are stored when they're being used.
And storage is where things are stored permanently.
Note that computer systems may contain far more components than this depending on their application, but they all do have this in common, processor, memory, and storage.
Sometimes computer parts may be given acronyms or known by different names.
For example, a processor may be called a central processing unit.
This is often shortened to the acronym CPU.
There are also two types of main memory.
So we have one type of memory called Random Access Memory that we've introduced already and that's often shortened to RAM.
The second type of main memory is called Read-Only Memory and is often shortened to ROM.
So two types of memory, RAM and ROM.
And that can get a little bit confusing because they're very similar terms. So to recap, second type of main memory is called Read-Only Memory and is often shortened to ROM.
RAM is a type of temporary memory that stores data and programs while a computer is in use.
RAM allows the system to work quickly, but its contents are lost when the computer is turned off.
Processors can read from and write to RAM, allowing them to quickly access and store the data needed to run programs and perform tasks.
ROM is different to RAM because it's permanent memory that stores it essential instructions for starting up the computer.
The data in ROM cannot be changed easily and is not lost when the power is turned off.
And Laura says, "I think we forgot to mention the thing that gives all computers the instructions on what to do." Can you think of it? Andeep has a question.

It may perform input or output of data.
It might control program flow.
When you open a game, the processor executes the game's instructions.
When you open a web browser, the processor executes the instructions from the program.
Whatever program you open, the processor executes the instructions to make it run.
Time for a question.
Which parts of a computer carries out instructions and makes decisions? Is it A, storage? B, power supply? Or C, processor? That's right, the answer is processor.
So the processor is the part of a computer that carries out instructions and makes decisions.
The RAM is the component that stores the programs and data currently in use by the processor.
So this is a picture of what a piece of RAM looks like within a computer.
So a computer may contain several of these depending on how much RAM it's running.
So RAM is temporary, fast, and works with the processor.
Remember that RAM is short for Random Access Memory.
When typing a document, the text is stored in RAM while you're working.
RAM is volatile.
This means its contents are lost when the power is off.
So Sam's got a question.

Because if RAM is volatile and the contents are lost when the power is off, how do you save your work? When you save your work, the data is moved into storage.
Storage is where a computer saves data and files so they can be used again at another time.
Storage is persistent, which means it retains its content when the power is turned off.
Note that storage devices are generally much slower than RAM.
And on this slide here, you've got a picture of a magnetic hard drive, which is a type of storage device.
RAM is built and designed for speed so the processor can work quickly while a program is running.
Storage is designed to hold large amounts of data, but takes longer to access.
There are many types of storage devices.

So is an SD card, which you might find in a camera.
A hard disk drive, HDD, hard disk drive.
That's an example of a storage device.
A solid state drive, which is a different type of hard drive.
That's also an example of a storage device.
And optical discs such as CDs or DVDs are also storage devices.
Time for a question.

00:11:54.690 --> 00:11:57.510
Storage is where data and files are permanently kept,

213
00:11:57.510 --> 00:11:59.790
even when it's turned off.

214
00:11:59.790 --> 00:12:02.550
Program is the set of instructions that tells the computer

215
00:12:02.550 --> 00:12:04.170
what tasks to perform.

216
00:12:04.170 --> 00:12:06.240
And then finally, RAM temporary stores

217
00:12:06.240 --> 00:12:09.003
important data and instructions when in use.

218
00:12:12.060 --> 00:12:14.160
And the second part of your task, in your own words,

219
00:12:14.160 --> 00:12:18.093
describe the two differences between storage and RAM.

220
00:12:25.680 --> 00:12:27.150
So this is what you could have written.

221
00:12:27.150 --> 00:12:30.300
One difference is that RAM and storage are designed

222
00:12:30.300 --> 00:12:32.370
and used for different purposes.

223
00:12:32.370 --> 00:12:34.620
RAM is used to temporarily hold data

224
00:12:34.620 --> 00:12:36.780
that the computer is currently using,

225
00:12:36.780 --> 00:12:39.630
while storage is used to save data permanently,

226
00:12:39.630 --> 00:12:41.883
even when the computer is turned off.

227
00:12:42.870 --> 00:12:44.670
Another difference between RAM and storage

228
00:12:44.670 --> 00:12:45.963
is how fast they are.

229
00:12:46.830 --> 00:12:49.140
RAM is designed to work much faster than storage

230
00:12:49.140 --> 00:12:51.660
because it needs to quickly supply the processor

231
00:12:51.660 --> 00:12:55.023
with the data and instructions it needs to work efficiently.

232
00:13:00.300 --> 00:13:02.100
Let's move on to the second learning cycle,

233
00:13:02.100 --> 00:13:05.133
which is to explain how a computer executes a program.

234
00:13:08.250 --> 00:13:09.097
So Laura says,

235
00:13:09.097 --> 00:13:11.580
"I know that the processor executes instructions,

236
00:13:11.580 --> 00:13:14.247
but I wonder how it works with other components."

237
00:13:17.520 --> 00:13:20.490
A computer follows a cycle of fetching, decoding,

238
00:13:20.490 --> 00:13:23.010
and executing instructions stored in RAM

239
00:13:23.010 --> 00:13:24.933
to run a program step by step.

240
00:13:26.070 --> 00:13:28.020
So let's delve into that a bit further.

241
00:13:30.210 --> 00:13:32.280
The fetch-decode-execute cycle

242
00:13:32.280 --> 00:13:36.243
describes the basic operation of modern computer systems.

243
00:13:39.690 --> 00:13:40.830
To run any program,

244
00:13:40.830 --> 00:13:45.213
the instructions must be fetched, decoded, and executed.

245
00:13:48.660 --> 00:13:51.870
First, instructions are fetched one by one from RAM

246
00:13:51.870 --> 00:13:55.023
into the processor along with any data that's needed.

247
00:13:57.660 --> 00:13:59.700
So there's the memory feeding the processor

248
00:13:59.700 --> 00:14:01.683
with instructions and data.

249
00:14:04.830 --> 00:14:08.343
The processor decodes and executes each instruction.

250
00:14:10.800 --> 00:14:12.930
When decoding, the processor works out

251
00:14:12.930 --> 00:14:14.643
what the instruction means.

252
00:14:17.130 --> 00:14:20.283
Once decoded, the processor executes the instruction.

253
00:14:23.880 --> 00:14:26.040
When all instructions have been executed,

254
00:14:26.040 --> 00:14:28.713
any resulting data is moved into memory.

255
00:14:32.070 --> 00:14:34.170
So the processor has executed the instructions

256
00:14:34.170 --> 00:14:36.843
and the resulting data goes back into the memory.

257
00:14:39.510 --> 00:14:42.480
The fetch-decode-execute cycle is repeated

258
00:14:42.480 --> 00:14:44.733
for as long as the computer is running.

259
00:14:45.600 --> 00:14:47.040
So whenever you've got a computer running,

260
00:14:47.040 --> 00:14:48.780
this is happening all the time

261
00:14:48.780 --> 00:14:51.530
and it's happening really, really quickly all the time.

262
00:14:55.560 --> 00:14:57.600
Note that this is also sometimes referred to

263
00:14:57.600 --> 00:15:02.600
as the FDE cycle, so fetch-decode-execute, FDE.

264
00:15:07.080 --> 00:15:08.550
An analogy can help you remember

265
00:15:08.550 --> 00:15:10.410
how the parts will computer work together

266
00:15:10.410 --> 00:15:13.200
as a system to execute a program.

267
00:15:13.200 --> 00:15:14.600
So let's have a look at one.

268
00:15:15.840 --> 00:15:18.393
Consider how a knitter may knit a jumper.

269
00:15:21.150 --> 00:15:22.890
Knitting patterns, yarn supplies,

270
00:15:22.890 --> 00:15:26.310
half-finished and finished projects are kept on the shelves,

271
00:15:26.310 --> 00:15:27.180
so there's the shelves there

272
00:15:27.180 --> 00:15:28.980
on the right-hand side of the image,

273
00:15:31.110 --> 00:15:33.423
and we can think of those as storage shelves.

274
00:15:35.370 --> 00:15:38.103
This is like the storage for programs and data.

275
00:15:40.500 --> 00:15:42.390
When the knitter works on a project,

276
00:15:42.390 --> 00:15:44.220
the knitting pattern and materials

277
00:15:44.220 --> 00:15:46.140
are transferred to the work area

278
00:15:46.140 --> 00:15:49.110
where they can be kept handy for quick access.

279
00:15:49.110 --> 00:15:50.360
So there's the work area.

280
00:15:52.020 --> 00:15:53.160
And this is like the RAM

281
00:15:53.160 --> 00:15:56.820
where the program under execution is stored temporarily

282
00:15:56.820 --> 00:15:59.343
along with the required data and the processing.

283
00:16:00.210 --> 00:16:01.800
The knitter reads from the knitting pattern

284
00:16:01.800 --> 00:16:03.180
one instruction at a time

285
00:16:03.180 --> 00:16:04.770
and carries out the instruction,

286
00:16:04.770 --> 00:16:06.840
operating on the material at hand.

287
00:16:06.840 --> 00:16:09.540
So what do you think that might be representing?

288
00:16:09.540 --> 00:16:11.167
So there's the knitter,

289
00:16:11.167 --> 00:16:12.990
and the knitter is like the processor

290
00:16:12.990 --> 00:16:14.523
executing the instructions.

291
00:16:19.260 --> 00:16:20.580
Laura says, "Oh, that makes sense.

292
00:16:20.580 --> 00:16:23.670
So the processor fetches instructions from RAM,

293
00:16:23.670 --> 00:16:26.430
decodes them to work out what the instruction means,

294
00:16:26.430 --> 00:16:28.200
and then executes the instructions

295
00:16:28.200 --> 00:16:29.847
and then the cycle is repeated."

296
00:16:32.790 --> 00:16:34.980
So let's have a look at a question.

297
00:16:34.980 --> 00:16:39.180
What does the F stand for in the FDE cycle?

298
00:16:39.180 --> 00:16:41.160
Is it A, format?

299
00:16:41.160 --> 00:16:42.300
B, forward?

300
00:16:42.300 --> 00:16:43.743
Or C, fetch?

301
00:16:49.050 --> 00:16:50.460
That's right, it's fetch.

302
00:16:50.460 --> 00:16:55.460
So F stands for fetch in the fetch-decode-execute cycle.

303
00:16:59.640 --> 00:17:00.473
Another question.

304
00:17:00.473 --> 00:17:03.120
During the decode phase, the processor...

305
00:17:03.120 --> 00:17:06.003
Does it A, work out what the instruction means?

306
00:17:07.080 --> 00:17:09.930
B, send the result and data to memory?

307
00:17:09.930 --> 00:17:12.693
Or C, copies the program to storage?

308
00:17:18.240 --> 00:17:19.740
Well done, during the decode phase,

309
00:17:19.740 --> 00:17:22.413
the processor works out what the instructions mean.

310
00:17:26.970 --> 00:17:28.230
Now part one of your task,

311
00:17:28.230 --> 00:17:30.840
match up the stages of the FDE cycle

312
00:17:30.840 --> 00:17:32.130
with the correct description.

313
00:17:32.130 --> 00:17:34.110
So the three stages we've got

314
00:17:34.110 --> 00:17:37.440
are fetch, decode, and execute.

315
00:17:37.440 --> 00:17:39.210
And the descriptions we have

316
00:17:39.210 --> 00:17:42.030
are work out what the instruction means,

317
00:17:42.030 --> 00:17:44.100
do what the instruction says,

318
00:17:44.100 --> 00:17:46.350
gets the next instruction from RAM.

319
00:17:46.350 --> 00:17:48.813
So match up the terms to the descriptions.

320
00:17:54.240 --> 00:17:55.073
Okay, well done.

321
00:17:55.073 --> 00:17:59.160
So the fetch stage is get the next instructions from RAM.

322
00:17:59.160 --> 00:18:02.610
The decode stage is to work out what the instruction means.

323
00:18:02.610 --> 00:18:04.560
And then the execute stage

324
00:18:04.560 --> 00:18:06.543
is to do what the instruction says.

325
00:18:10.860 --> 00:18:13.530
And the second part of your task, in your own words,

326
00:18:13.530 --> 00:18:16.320
explain how a computer executes a program.

327
00:18:16.320 --> 00:18:17.610
And there's a tip here.

328
00:18:17.610 --> 00:18:20.220
If it helps, you could use an analogy to help explain.

329
00:18:20.220 --> 00:18:22.500
For example, how the FDE cycle

330
00:18:22.500 --> 00:18:24.423
is similar to a chef cooking a meal.

331
00:18:31.380 --> 00:18:32.213
In your own words,

332
00:18:32.213 --> 00:18:34.530
explain how a computer executes a program.

333
00:18:34.530 --> 00:18:36.360
So just like a recipe tells a chef

334
00:18:36.360 --> 00:18:38.100
what steps to follow to make a dish,

335
00:18:38.100 --> 00:18:39.840
a program is a set of instructions

336
00:18:39.840 --> 00:18:41.523
that tells a computer what to do.

337
00:18:42.360 --> 00:18:44.760
The processor is like the chef because it reads

338
00:18:44.760 --> 00:18:46.530
and follows the instructions step by step

339
00:18:46.530 --> 00:18:48.420
to complete a task.

340
00:18:48.420 --> 00:18:50.460
The RAM is like the kitchen counter

341
00:18:50.460 --> 00:18:51.630
where ingredients are placed

342
00:18:51.630 --> 00:18:53.670
and prepared in a temporary workspace

343
00:18:53.670 --> 00:18:55.530
that holds everything a chef needs

344
00:18:55.530 --> 00:18:57.930
while following the recipe instructions.

345
00:18:57.930 --> 00:19:01.080
Storage in a computer is like a fridge in a kitchen

346
00:19:01.080 --> 00:19:03.630
because it holds data and programmed long term

347
00:19:03.630 --> 00:19:07.320
just like a fridge stores food until you're ready to use it.

348
00:19:07.320 --> 00:19:09.330
The chef takes each recipe instruction,

349
00:19:09.330 --> 00:19:11.043
understands it, and performs it.

350
00:19:11.910 --> 00:19:13.440
This is similar to how a processor

351
00:19:13.440 --> 00:19:15.570
fetches each instruction from RAM,

352
00:19:15.570 --> 00:19:17.280
decodes it into something it understands

353
00:19:17.280 --> 00:19:19.800
and then executes the instruction.

354
00:19:19.800 --> 00:19:21.060
After following all the steps,

355
00:19:21.060 --> 00:19:22.920
the chef produces a finished meal.

356
00:19:22.920 --> 00:19:25.530
And this is like how a computer produces output

357
00:19:25.530 --> 00:19:27.273
after executing a program.

358
00:19:32.490 --> 00:19:36.480
So here's a summary of this lesson Computer Architecture.

359
00:19:36.480 --> 00:19:38.880
So every computer has the same basic parts,

360
00:19:38.880 --> 00:19:41.283
such as processor, RAM, and storage.

361
00:19:42.450 --> 00:19:46.200
The Central Processing Unit, or CPU, executes instructions

362
00:19:46.200 --> 00:19:48.783
and controls other parts of a computer system.

363
00:19:49.680 --> 00:19:52.560
All computers use the fetch-decode-execute cycle

364
00:19:52.560 --> 00:19:54.933
as the basic way they execute programs.

365
00:19:57.120 --> 00:19:58.770
Thank you very much for joining me

366
00:19:58.770 --> 00:20:01.620
for today's Oak Academy lesson.

367
00:20:01.620 --> 00:20:03.120
I hope you enjoyed learning along with me

368
00:20:03.120 --> 00:20:05.753
and I look forward to seeing you again in the future.

lessonKeywords.description: an electronic device that processes data and performs tasks
a set of commands that can be run by a computer in order for it to do a task

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Computers follow instructions called programs to perform tasks.
Programs tell the computer how to process data, such as numbers, text, or images.
A general-purpose computer can run many different programs, unlike a single-purpose device, which is built for one job.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: General-purpose computers can run many programs, but single-purpose computers are designed to do one task very efficiently.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All computers can do everything equally well.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe how general-purpose computers use programs to process different types of data and perform a wide range of tasks.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Try to make the lesson interactive by having students list devices they know and decide if they are single-purpose or general-purpose. Or, show pictures and ask students to guess which type of device it is and why.

lessonKeywords.description: to manage or direct the behaviour of a system or process
the main software that manages a computer’s hardware and allows other programs to run
the physical parts of a computer that you can see and touch

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The operating system is a special program that controls the computer.
The operating system helps programs execute by managing memory, CPU time, and input/output.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: What you see on the screen is the graphical interface, but the operating system includes a lot more behind the scenes such as memory management, file systems, device control etc.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The operating system is just what you see on the screen.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how operating systems control computers and manage resources.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Use analogies to compare the operating system to a school principal or office manager.  Explain they run the whole building, manage what everyone is doing, and keep things organised. This is like how an operating system controls programs, manages files, and helps everything work together.

lessons.transcript_sentences:
Hi, my name's Mr. Hall, and welcome to this Oak National Academy lesson, which is called "The operating system," and it's taken from the unit, "Computer systems and data science." Thank you for joining me for this lesson, and I look forward to learning with you today.
The outcome of this lesson is "I can explain how operating systems control computers and manage resources." So let's get started.
We have three keywords in this lesson.
So the first keyword is control, and control means to manage or direct the behaviour of a system or process.
So that's control.
Then we have operating system or OS for short.
The main software that manages computer resources.
That's operating system or OS.
And finally, hardware.
So hardware is the physical parts of a computer that you can see and touch.
That's hardware.
So there's our three keywords, control operating system or OS, and hardware.
We have two learning cycles in this lesson.
So first, you're going to define an operating system, and then later in the lesson we'll move on to explain how an operating system manages resources.
So let's get started with the first learning cycle, define an operating system.
So Andeep has a question for Jun.
"Do you know how many programmes can be executed at the same time?" And Jun says, "Well, I remember a processor can only execute one instruction at a time.
So I think it's one." Let's see if he's correct.
He is, and we'll look at why now.
At any given time, a single core processor executes one instruction that is part of one programme.
So one processor, one instruction, one programme.
But Laura says, "But I often have lots of programmes open at the same time.
How does that work?" So there's an example.
You can see there's at least four programmes open on that desktop.
There may even be more open that you can't see.
So several programmes open at the same time.
So if a single processor can execute one instruction, one programme, how can we run multiple programmes at once? So let's have a look.
So a single processor can be made to alternate between executing the instructions of different programmes.
This makes it look like multiple programmes are being executed at the same time, but actually, the processor is still only executing one programme at a time.
So it's very quickly switching between those programmes, but only ever executing one instruction per programme at any one time.
A single core processor that switches between executing programmes is similar to how a single builder can only work on one wall at a time, but could quickly switch between building different walls.
So we have four walls being built, but they can only be built one at a time.
Currently the speed, so that's the clock ticks per second, is at 1.
So each wall is being built with one instruction happening per second.
I can increase the speed slightly.
So if I go to 6 ticks, you can see that still, there's four walls being built.
It's still only one instruction per time, but it's happening quicker.
And I can go right up to a really fast speed, say 92, and you can see that it's still four walls, one instruction per time, but much quicker because the clock speed is quicker.
So have a look at that simulation and that gives you an idea of how a processor can manage one instruction for one programme at any one time.
But the faster the processor, the more instructions it will be able to handle.
So Andeep has another question now, "But what happens if a processor has multiple cores?" In that case, each core can execute instructions from a different programme.
In the brick building analogy, this is like having multiple workers building a wall each, so it'd be a quicker process.
So there you see, we have potentially four bricklayers each building their own wall.
So you can see that would be four times as fast as a single processor if they were all working at the same speed.
So Andeep says, "So the processor executes the programme instructions, but what controls the processor, which is a really good question.
And Jun asked, "And what controls were the programmes and data are stored in the RAM?" And the answer to both those questions is the operating system is the main software that controls how a computer works.
So let's have a look at the operating system in a bit more detail.
There are several very well-known operating systems that are installed on different devices like laptops, tablets, and phones.
Can you think of any operating systems that start up when you turn on a computer or a phone? So here's some common ones that you may have come across.
So the first logo is for the Android operating system, which typically you'll see on phones and mobile devices.
Then we have OS, which is Apple's operating system.
So you'll typically see that on Apple devices.
And then finally, Windows on the right-hand side, which you will see on desktop PCs and laptop PCs.
The operating system is the first software that loads when a computer starts and serves as a base for launching and running applications.
The main purpose of an operating system is to allow users and applications to interact with and control computers and its hardware.
The operating system controls the computer's hardware by acting as a bridge between the physical components and the software, allowing them to work together effectively.
It controls key parts of the computer's hardware such as the processor, RAM, storage devices, and input, output, and peripheral devices.
So there's a lot of work for the operating system to do to make sure all these different components can work effectively together.
Sam says, "Without an operating system, you wouldn't be able to launch a programme." Not only that, you wouldn't even be able to type, click, or view files.
So you wouldn't be able to use your keyboard, you wouldn't be able to use your mouse, and you wouldn't be able to open anything.
Nothing would work.
The operating system also provides the graphical user interface, and this is often shortened to GUI, for the G, the U, and the I, so GUI.
A GUI allows users to interact with the computer through visual elements like Windows, icons, buttons, and menus instead of typing commands.
A GUI makes it easier for most users to control and use the computer.
So before GUIs were around, you had to type everything in terms of commands just on a single line without any graphics, icons, Windows, or buttons to help you.
So GUIs are really useful to make computers easier to control.
So let's have a look at an analogy now.
An operating system is a bit like the conductor in an orchestra.
Just as a conductor cues the musicians, the operating system controls programmes and devices so everything runs smoothly.
In an orchestra, a conductor controls the tempo and tells instruments when to play.
This is similar to an operating system that controls when and how different programmes and devices operate.
Another thing a conductor does is to communicate the musical vision to the orchestra.
In a similar way, the operating system acts as a messenger between the user and the computer's hardware.
So if an update is required, the operating system will tell the user that that needs to happen.
Time for a question.
What is the main software that controls how a computer works? Is it A, the random access memory or RAM? Is it B, the graphical user interface or GUI? Or is it C, the operating system or OS? Well done.
The answer is C, it's the operating system that controls how a computer works.
Now, time for a true or false question.
Every computer runs the same operating system.
Is that true or false? Well done.
It's false.
Can you explain why? And it's false because there are many different operating systems that can be installed on different devices like laptops, tablets, and phones.
And we saw examples of three, so Android, OS, and Windows.
Some of those are some of the most commonly used operating systems. Now, time for your task.
First, in your own words, write one or two sentences to describe what an operating system is, and then state two reasons why an operating system is important for using a computer.
Okay, so the answer to the first question in your own words, write one or two sentences to describe what an operating system is, you could have written something like this.
"The operating system is the main software that controls how a computer works.
It is the first software that loads when a computer starts and serves as a base for launching, and running applications, and controlling hardware." And for the second part of the task, state two reasons why an operating system is important for using a computer, and you could have written something like this.
"An operating system is important because it controls programmes, hardware, and devices so that everything runs smoothly as a system." Another reason is that the operating system provides a graphical user interface or GUI, which makes it easier for users to control and use the computer through visual elements like icons, buttons, and menus.
Now, it is time to move on to the second learning cycle, which is to explain how an operating system manages resources.
Sam asks, "How is an operating system like traffic lights?" Let's have a look.
An operating system is like traffic lights because it controls the flow of data and instructions.
This is similar to how traffic lights control which cars move to prevent crashes and confusion.
So at a junction, if one light is red and the other is green, then only one line of traffic can move.
And by stopping the other line of traffic, you stop crashes and confusion where two lines of traffic might cross.
So that's how traffic lights help to control traffic in a similar way to the way an operating system controls the flow of data and instructions on a computer.
The operating system directly manages a number of computer resources such as the random access memory, the processor time, input/output devices, and ensures all running programmes get the resources they need without crashing or interfering with each other.
So it has a crucial role in the running of the computer.
The operating system manages memory by keeping track of where each program's data is stored in RAM.
And Sam says, "This ensures that programmes do not interfere with each other's allocation of RAM space." Without memory management, programmes could override each other's data leading to crashes, errors, or lost information.
The operating system manages processor time by deciding which programmes or tasks get to use the CPU and for how long.
And Jun is helpfully reminding us that a single core processor can only execute a single instruction at a time for a single programme.
So the operating system manages which programme the CPU will be handling at any one time.
By allocating individual processor time to programmes, the computer can appear to run multiple applications smoothly without freezing or crashing.
If the operating system didn't control CPU time, programmes could try and use the processor at the same time and that would cause conflicts.
The computer might freeze or become very slow because the CPU wouldn't know which tasks to focus on or when.
And sometimes you may have seen computers crashing or blue screening, as you can see on the picture there, and this could be because there's some kind of conflict within the CPU, so it doesn't always work perfectly.
The operating system manages input and output devices by controlling how data is sent to and received from devices such as keyboards, mice, printers, and monitors.
It coordinates communication between the hardware devices and the software.
If an operating system didn't manage input and output devices, programmes wouldn't know how to send or receive data from hardware.
And this could lead to all sorts of problems. It could mean input going to the wrong programme.
It could mean output not showing up correctly.
And it could lead to conflicts between programmes trying to use the same device at once.
Operating systems are similar to traffic lights because they control the flow of tasks in a computer, just like how traffic lights control the flow of traffic.

lessonKeywords.description: a networked computer that stores and provides web pages and other data on request
Hypertext Transfer Protocol, a set of rules that allows data such as web pages to be sent and received across the WWW
the Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure is a set of rules that allows data to be encrypted and exchanged securely via the WWW
a segment of data, usually part of a larger message

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The World Wide Web (WWW) relies on web browsers, web servers and web pages to deliver information and services.
Explain how the internet uses packets to efficiently and reliably transmit data across networks.
The HTTP protocol is used govern how data is exchanged between web browsers and servers.
The HTTPS protocol provides secure communication between web browsers and servers.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Data packets are split and will be sent using the most efficient route at the time which often changes. Packets include data parts so they can be reassembled at the destination as long as the order of the packets is identified before being sent.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Data packets from a complete message always follow the same route to their destination. They are then put back together in the order they are received.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how the components of the World Wide Web (WWW) work together to display web pages.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Help pupils visualise the process of breaking down a large amount of data into smaller packets by having them cut up and reassemble a printed image. They need to understand that the order of the packets should be determined by using a sequence number to help with reordering upon delivery.

lessonKeywords.description: uses a cable to connect a device to a network
the transmission of data between devices without using physical cables or wires
the maximum amount of data that can be transferred over a communication channel

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Wired and wireless networks have different advantages and disadvantages, making them suitable for different situations.
Bandwidth determines how much data can be sent at a time, affecting the overall time taken to complete a transfer.
Different online activities require different amounts data be transfered.
Different mobile data technologies provide varying levels of bandwidth, which affects the quality of network activities.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Bandwidth is the maximum amount of data that can be transmitted at a time, not the time it takes to reach from one point to another. Higher bandwidth reduces the total transfer time of data but this is only noticable when there is a lot to transfer.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Bandwidth is the speed of data being transmitted across a network. The higher the bandwidth, the faster data can be transferred between points in a network.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can compare the performance of different types of network connections.

teacherTips.teacherTip: You may want to use an analogy of motorway lanes for bandwidth. More lanes mean more cars can travel side by side without traffic jams. Higher bandwidth is like having more lanes on your internet connection.

lessonKeywords.description: a group of devices connected together, wirelessly or using cables, to enable communication
a set of rules used to allow devices to communicate with each other
a unique number assigned to each device on a network, used to identify it and allow it to send or receive data

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Protocols are sets of rules that are followed to allow communication to take place.
IP adresses are given to devices on a local network.
IP addresses need to be unique on the same network.
The IP addresses of both the receiver and sender need be added to every network message.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Protocols are essential for all sorts of activities, not just email or browsing websites. Protocols are also needed for streaming movies, playing online games, making video calls, etc. Anything being sent across a network needs to follow a protocol.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Computers only need protocols when sending emails or accessing websites.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how devices on a computer network use protocols to communicate.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Discuss how protocols are used in everyday communication, such as traffic lights, phone calls or even raising your hand in class. This helps students connect the concept to familiar experiences and understand the importance of protocols in various contexts.

lessonKeywords.description: a group of devices connected together, wirelessly or using cables, to enable communication
a computer that stores, manages and shares files, data and resources in a network
a device that requests services, files or resources from a server on a network
a device that manages the flow of data between computer networks

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Devices on networks connect for communication and resource sharing.
Networks rely on specialised hardware.
Devices on networks perform different roles in order to exchange information.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Servers, clients and routers have distinct roles and functionalities in a network. They are not interchangeable and serve different purposes.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: On a network, servers, clients and routers have the same purpose.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe a local network and its components.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Discuss the benefits of a local network in your learners' own lives. Ask them to think about how they use networks at home or at school for communication and sharing resources.

lessonKeywords.description: a network of everyday devices that are connected to the internet and can communicate with each other
the protection of an individual's personal information and the control over how it is used

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The internet of things (IoT) connects everyday objects to the internet, enabling them to collect and share data.
Personal information is information collected about a person.
Understand that connected devices can gather and share your personal information, which can impact your privacy.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: IoT are everyday devices that are connected to the internet and can communicate with each other. They might not collect data for the same purpose but they can collect information about how people use the devices.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The internet of things (IoT) is only about smart homes and appliances.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain how devices share data in the internet of things (IoT) and how this can have an impact on privacy.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Find examples of 'free' internet services that pupils might use. Discuss what information could be collected as part of their use and then ask the class to decide how companies make money from these free services.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The internet is a global network of networks that shares information using the World Wide Web (WWW).
The WWW is a system of web pages that we access using the internet.
The internet provides a platform for a wide range of services.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: The World Wide Web is a service that is offered over the internet. The internet is the network that transfers data whilst the World Wide Web is the system of sharing information that people use.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The internet is the same as the World Wide Web.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can explain the difference between the internet and the World Wide Web and describe some of the services the internet offers.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Ask the students to create a mind map or concept map to illustrate the different services offered over the internet and how they relate to the World Wide Web. Make sure that pupils understand how much we use computer networks as part of our everyday lives.

lessonKeywords.description: to generate high-quality images from a 3D model or scene by taking into account lighting, materials and other properties
a rendering technique that creates realistic images by simulating the paths of light rays as they interact with objects in a scene
to save image, animation, model or scene data in a file format that can be used by other software or applications

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Rendering is the process of generating high-quality images from a 3D scene or object.
Render engines should be chosen based on the requirements of the project.
Ray tracing simulates the way light interacts with objects and environments.
Rendered images and animations can be exported out of Blender.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Render engines and settings should be chosen with consideration to the requirements of the project. This may include considering factors such as time constraints and hardware limitations.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: The most detailed renders should always be produced.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can render and export an animation.

teacherTips.teacherTip: If you have access to high-specification computers, consider instructing learners to use the Cycles render engine instead of EEVEE for Task B. Learners could then compare and discuss the merits and disadvantages of rendering animations with EEVEE and Cycles.

lessonKeywords.description: to transform a 2D shape into a 3D object by extending it along a path or direction
a surface made up of three or more edges
a line connecting two vertices
a point where two or more edges or lines meet

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: 2D shapes can be extruded to create a 3D object.
3D models are composed of faces, edges and vertices.
Additional geometry can be added to a model using the loop cut tool.
Materials can be applied to individual or groups of faces.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Having only previously used object mode, learners may be unaware that geometry such as vertices, edges and faces can all be directly modified in edit mode. Working in edit mode gives a modeller greater freedom to create more complex models.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: 3D models are all made up of simple shapes that are scaled, moved and rotated.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can create and detail complex 3D models.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage learners to explore Blender and get used to the toolsets and workspace. Learners will need to be comfortable working between object mode and edit mode, so get them to practise switching between the two modes.

lessons.transcript_sentences:
Hello, my name is Mr. Coxhead and it's great to see you joining me for today's lesson that's called Key Frame Animation and Parenting Objects.
Let's get started.
The outcome for this lesson is I can create an animation using key frames.
And here are the key words.
Timeline.
A visual representation of time on which frames can be sequenced.
Key frame.
A marker that captures the most important positions or states of an object.
Tweening.
The process of automatically generating frames between two points.
And parenting.
The process of nesting objects within other objects.
There are two parts to this lesson today.
The first one, we're going to look at how we can animate with key frames, and in the second part, we're going to look at how we compare and organise objects to keep our scene tidy and to make it easy to work with.
Let's get started on the lesson.
Look at the 3D model below.
What shapes do you think we'll use to create the model? Pause the video if you'd like some time to think.
So the model was created with three cones under cylinder.
Remember, these are what we call primitive shapes and they're usually the starting point to get the main shape of our models.
Animation is the process of capturing still images that can be replayed to create the illusion of movement.
There are five main types of animation.
Traditional or cell animation, 2D vector animation, 3D animation, motion graphics, and stop motion.
Let's take a look at these types of animation.
So traditional cell animation, each frame is hand drawn on paper or digitally on a computer.
Here we can see we're playing back the frames at one frame per second.
When we play them back at speed, it gives the illusion of movement and this is the oldest form of animation and it's what was used on the early cartoons.
The faster we play these speeds back, the smoother the animation.
In 2D vector animation, images can be manipulated in software to speed up the production process, and this technique is often used on websites, TV shows, video games and cartoons.
In stop motion animation, physical objects are moved before each frame is manually captured.
And materials such as clay and plasticine are ideal choices for models in this style of animation.
In motion graphics, use of shapes, text and objects add impact to a message.
Motion graphics are often created to add impact to video titles, logo graphics, and digital advertisements.
In 3D animation, computers are used to create moving images in a 3D environment.
So this type of animation can produce very high quality 3D content for use in movies, visualisations and video games.
In 3D animation, a timeline is used to visualise the sequence of animations.
This animation starts at frame one and it ends on frame 24.
It also has a total of 24 individual frames.
Key frames can be set on a timeline, and a key frame is a point that defines the start and end of a smooth transition of an object.
In this example, key frames have been set on frames one, 12 and 24.
Tweening is used to automatically generate frames in between the key frames.
In this example, tweening has been used to create frames two to 11 and 13 to 23, and this has created the illusion of a smooth movement between those key frames.
And tweening saves animators lots of time and effort.
There are several advantages to using keyframe animation such as faster to make the animations, easier to edit, smoother animations and repeatable.
So you can use the same animation for somebody walking in a different shot.
Many different applications can be used to create 3D animations.
Blender is an open source 3D modelling and animating application that is free to use.
You can use whatever software you have access to in this lesson, but just keep in mind they may look a little bit different than the examples when I use Blender.
Keyframes can be added to an object's timeline by selecting an object and pressing the I key.
Each object in a 3D scene has its own timeline, and this means that more than one object can be animated in the scene.
Key frames can be edited on a timeline to improve the animation sequence and playback.
3D animating with key frames can be used to add realism, dynamics and fun to 3D models and scenes.
Here's a video clip on how to animate a snowball.
Here we are inside of Blender and we're going to take a look at how we can animate a snowball into the snowman's head.

And proportional editing is a useful technique to give a 3D model a realistic organic feel.
Proportional editing is a way of modifying selected elements while having an effect on other nearby elements.
When a vertex, edge or face is moved, others within a radius will move proportionally.
And proportional editing creates smoother natural-looking 3D models.
In Blender, proportional editing can be enabled by clicking on this icon from the top toolbar.
Edit mode must be enabled to proportionally edit vertices, edges or faces.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Selection is used when there is more than one possible path for a program to follow.
Selection is carried out using if, elif and else statements.
A selection statement will check if a condition returns as True or False.
Multi-path selection is used when there is more than one path for a program to follow.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Selection statements can be used to control program flow, so some lines of code can be skipped to  follow a different path through the program.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: A program follows a sequence of instructions and will run all lines of code.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe how selection statements are used in programs to control program flow.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Pupils may find the come across syntax errors with missing : and indentation in selection statements. Encourage them to self check programs for these pitfalls.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Software engineers are often given a set of project requirements that they have to turn into code to create a solution.
A larger problem is decomposed into smaller subproblems to make it easier to solve.
A flowchart or pseudocode is often used to design a system before it is created.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Individual subproblems can be approached separately and tested to ensure they work before moving onto the next part. It helps to know parts of a program work as intended.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All parts of a solution must be coded at the same time and tested that it works once coding has finished.

lessonKeywords.description: a symbol or word that instructs the computer to perform a specific calculation or action
an expression that results in a numeric value
sometimes known as floor division, is when any remainder of a division is discarded
an operation that gives you the remainder when one number is divided by another

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Arithmetic expressions are used to calculate values.
Arithmetic expressions can be used in selection statements. Expressions either return as True or False.
In real division there is no remainder because the entire value is divided.
Integer division is when any remainder of a division is discarded.
Modulo division (MOD) will return only the remainder of a division.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: There are three types of division in programming; real, integer and modulo division. Each deal with remainder values differently and will be useful in different ways in programming.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Just like addition, subtraction and multiplication there is only one type of division in programming.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use a variety of arithmetic operators in a program.

teacherTips.teacherTip: This lesson requires pupils to understand the order of precedence of operations. Spend some time ensuring pupils understand the concepts covered in the maths curriculum before moving on to implementing in programs.

lessonKeywords.description: a block of code where a selection block is placed within another selection block

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Selection statements with conditions can be nested inside another selection statement.
Nested selection statements are used to implement complex branching logic.
If a condition of a main selection block evaluates to True, it leads to sub-conditions which are inside the main block.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Selection statements can can continue to be nested in further selection blocks to provide more complex conditions for which specific code will be executed.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: A nested selection statement can only have one nested selection block.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can trace and modify code in a program that uses nested selection.

teacherTips.teacherTip: The second part of the lesson requires pupils to modify an existing program. Encourage learners to run the code a few times to investigate how it works before answering the questions.

lessonKeywords.description: an expression that combines relational and logical operators

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Logical operators are often used when you need to evaluate multiple relational expressions to return a single value.
Logical expressions return as either True or False. The three basic logical operators are and, or, and not.
Logical expressions can be used in selection statements.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Logical expressions can combine relational and logical operators to check multiple values or inputs.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: A logical expression can only check one value.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can use logical operators to build more complex selection statements.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Comparing values of objects is a useful way to visualise the use of realtional operators. Props in the classroom help make these comparisons more concrete.

lessons.lessonTitle: Getting the most out of an LLM
lessons.unitTitle: Using data science and AI tools effectively and safely

lessonKeywords.description: the input question, instruction, or message you give to a large language model (LLM)
when something is unclear or too general to be useful
the extra information you give to help the LLM interpret your prompt better
using knowledge and skills to design and create things that solve problems or make life easier

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The performance of LLMs is highly dependent on how users craft their prompts.
Prompts should be specific and clear to enable the model to interpret what you want.
Prompts should provide relevant context or examples so the model can generate more accurate and tailored responses.
LLMs can reflect biases from their training data, so responses should be critically evaluated and cross-checked.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: LLMs work best when you give them clear, specific and well-structured prompts. The quality of the input directly affects the quality of the output; this process of designing and refining inputs to get better results is called prompt engineering.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: You can just type anything into an LLM and it will always give the best answer.

lessons.pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe how to improve LLM output and use prompt engineering to improve LLM output.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Ask learners to use a vague prompt with a chatbot. Then get them to engineer and improve their prompt by adding specific details, relevant context and stating the format they would like the output to be in. Then compare the before and after outputs to see how their changes improved the response.

and saving time and reducing errors in the output.

215
00:12:10.620 --> 00:12:13.200
There are many ways to use prompt engineering

216
00:12:13.200 --> 00:12:15.123
to improve LLM output.

217
00:12:16.080 --> 00:12:21.080
A simple four-step process can help you get good results:

218
00:12:21.300 --> 00:12:24.480
decide exactly what you need,

219
00:12:24.480 --> 00:12:27.483
write clear and specific instructions,

220
00:12:28.560 --> 00:12:31.173
add context and format,

221
00:12:32.160 --> 00:12:33.693
and test and improve.

222
00:12:35.940 --> 00:12:39.960
You might start prompt engineering by identifying your goal

223
00:12:39.960 --> 00:12:42.453
and deciding exactly what you need.

224
00:12:43.417 --> 00:12:46.380
"Be clear about exactly what you want to achieve

225
00:12:46.380 --> 00:12:49.707
by using the chatbot application or LLM."

226
00:12:51.270 --> 00:12:54.963
Think about the topic and the level of detail that you need.

227
00:12:56.700 --> 00:12:59.580
Then, write a clear prompt that describes

228
00:12:59.580 --> 00:13:03.453
what you want from the LLM using specific words.

229
00:13:04.650 --> 00:13:08.010
Sofia says, "Remember to avoid vague language

230
00:13:08.010 --> 00:13:10.650
and be direct with your instructions."

231
00:13:10.650 --> 00:13:12.453
That's a really good tip from Sofia.

232
00:13:13.800 --> 00:13:17.130
Add clear formatting cues to the prompt

233
00:13:17.130 --> 00:13:19.353
to shape the output of the LLM.

234
00:13:20.460 --> 00:13:23.190

235

236

237
00:13:30.570 --> 00:13:34.080

238
00:13:34.080 --> 00:13:38.370

239
00:13:38.370 --> 00:13:41.097

240
00:13:42.390 --> 00:13:45.240
Adding context to the prompt will guide the LLM

241
00:13:45.240 --> 00:13:48.480
to generate output that is more accurate, relevant,

242
00:13:48.480 --> 00:13:50.253
and suited to your needs.

243

249

250

256

257
00:14:47.070 --> 00:14:50.643

258
00:14:52.830 --> 00:14:56.730

262

278
00:16:04.980 --> 00:16:07.050
Developing prompt engineering skills

279

00:21:33.750 --> 00:21:37.650
